messages.text: I accidentally changed ip address to static and now I cannot connect to miner.  How do I reset to default?

Hi, I'm H., HeliumDeploy's technical specialist. Sarah passed this over to me.

Good news: a bad static IP is almost always recoverable without losing anything else.

One thing first so I give you the right reset: **which miner is it?** (Harlo B30, a NerdQX / NerdOctaxe / Bitaxe, a Hammer, Nexus, or something else?)

In the meantime, the quickest non-destructive check: the miner is probably still alive on the static address you typed, just on the wrong subnet. If you remember the address you entered, tell me it plus your router's address (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1) and we can often just reach it again instead of resetting.

If you would rather go straight to a reset:

1. On an Axe-type board (NerdQX, NerdOctaxe, Bitaxe), power it on, press and hold the **BOOT** button about 5 seconds until the screen shows it is clearing settings. It comes back up in DHCP and broadcasts its own Wi-Fi AP for setup.
2. On a Harlo B30, there is a recessed **reset** pinhole next to the Ethernet port. With the unit powered on, hold it about 10 seconds with a paperclip until the LED blinks, then let go. Network settings go back to DHCP, pool config stays.

Tell me the model and I will confirm the exact one before you press anything.
Hammer dc06

Thanks, that helps. The D.06 uses a Bitmain-style control board, so you have two ways in.

**Fastest, no reset:** if you remember the static IP you entered, set your PC to the same subnet temporarily (for example if you typed 10.0.0.50, give your PC 10.0.0.51 / 255.255.255.0), plug the PC straight into the miner with an Ethernet cable, and browse to that IP. You can then set it back to DHCP from the Network page.

**Network reset:** on the control board, next to the Ethernet port, there is a small **reset** button and an **IP Report** button.

1. Leave the miner powered on.
2. Press and hold **reset** for about 5 seconds, until the lights blink, then release.
3. Wait about 2 minutes for it to reboot. It comes back on DHCP.
4. Press the **IP Report** button briefly, or check your router's DHCP client list, to find the new address.

That 5 second press only clears the network config. A long hold (around 30 seconds) is a full factory reset and also wipes your pool settings, so avoid it unless you have to.

Which do you want to try first? And tell me what the LEDs do when you press reset, that tells me whether the control board is responding.
Can’t find the reset button

No problem, it is easy to miss. On the DC06 everything is on the end panel where the Ethernet cable plugs in.

1. Look at that panel with the Ethernet port facing you.
2. Right beside the port you should see two tiny holes or micro buttons, often unlabeled or marked **RST** and **IP**. They are smaller than a pencil tip, so a paperclip or SIM tool is what you need.
3. Some DC06 units have them recessed behind the mesh, so shine a phone light in.

If you can send me a photo of that end panel, I will point at the exact spot.

While you look, the method that needs no button at all usually wins here:

1. Plug your laptop straight into the miner with an Ethernet cable.
2. Set the laptop to a manual IP on the same subnet as the address you typed into the miner (same first three numbers, different last number, mask 255.255.255.0).
3. Open a browser to the miner's static IP and set the Network page back to DHCP.

Do you remember what static IP you entered? If yes, give me that and I will give you the exact laptop settings to type in.

One more option at this hour: our Discord is very active late, https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , and JD (@nullhashrate) knows the DC06 board layout down to the solder joints.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)
Handed to the team · Need JD to confirm the exact reset button location and hold time on this DC06 bo

Thanks, that photo settles it. I owe you a correction: your DC06 is not the Bitmain style control board I described, it is the Axe style board with the colour LCD, so there is no RST / IP pinhole beside the Ethernet jack. Sorry for sending you hunting.

Good news, that board tells you its own address.

1. Look at the LCD. It rotates through several pages, one of which shows the network info including the IP address the miner is actually using.
2. If it does not rotate on its own, give it 30 to 60 seconds, or power cycle it and watch the first few screens after boot.
3. Tell me the IP it shows and I will give you the exact laptop settings to reach it, then we put it back on DHCP from the Network page in the web UI.

If the screen shows no IP or shows 0.0.0.0, the next move is the **BOOT** button on the board (small tactile button on the ESP32 side, usually near the USB-C port, not by the Ethernet jack). Held about 5 seconds on a running unit it clears the saved network settings and the miner comes back up asking for setup over its own Wi-Fi AP. Do not press anything yet, let us read the screen first.

I have also flagged this to JD, our hardware lead, so he can confirm the exact button and hold time for your board revision. The team picks it up tomorrow at 10am ET and the answer comes to your email.

Faster tonight if you want it: our Discord, https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , and ping @nullhashrate (JD). He and the community are active late.
I don’t have a laptop only a phone and ipad

No laptop needed. An iPad does this perfectly, and it can stay on Wi-Fi as long as the miner is plugged into the same router.

Here is the trick: we give the iPad a second identity on the miner's subnet.

On the iPad:
1. Settings, then Wi-Fi.
2. Tap the blue **(i)** next to your network name.
3. Tap **Configure IP**, choose **Manual**.
4. Enter an IP in the same range as the miner, subnet mask 255.255.255.0, and leave Router blank or set it to the miner's range .1 address.
5. Save, then open Safari and go to the miner's IP.

For example, if you set the miner to 10.0.0.50, you give the iPad 10.0.0.60 / 255.255.255.0.

Two things I need from you:
1. The static IP you typed into the miner, or whatever IP the LCD is showing now.
2. Whether the miner is wired to the router or on Wi-Fi.

When you are done, set Configure IP back to **Automatic** on the iPad, and set the miner back to DHCP in its Network page.
It is on WiFi I will send pic

Perfect, send it over.

Ideally a shot of the LCD page that shows the network info or IP address. If the screen rotates, just grab it when the IP appears.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)

That is exactly what I needed. The miner is alive, on Wi-Fi, and sitting at **192.168.1.100**.

First, the easy test:

1. On your iPad or phone, open Safari.
2. Go to **http://192.168.1.100**

If the web UI loads, you are done, just go to the Network settings and switch it back to DHCP.

If it does not load, your home network is on a different range, and we fix it like this:

1. Settings, Wi-Fi, tap the blue **(i)** next to your network.
2. Read me the **IP Address** line it shows for the iPad (something like 192.168.0.14 or 10.0.0.23).

Tell me what happens with the Safari test, and that iPad IP address if it fails.
Safari test failed could not find server

Expected. That means your home network uses a different range than 192.168.1.x.

Give me the one number I need:

1. Settings, then Wi-Fi.
2. Tap the blue **(i)** next to your network name.
3. Read the **IP Address** line (and the **Router** line while you are there).

Send me those two and I will give you the exact values to type into Configure IP > Manual so the iPad can reach 192.168.1.100. Then we set the miner back to DHCP and you put the iPad back to Automatic.

That explains everything. Your network is 10.0.0.x and the miner is parked on 192.168.1.100, so they cannot see each other even though both are on the same Wi-Fi.

Fix on the iPad:

1. Settings, Wi-Fi, blue **(i)** next to your network.
2. Tap **Configure IP**, choose **Manual**.
3. IP Address: **192.168.1.50**
4. Subnet Mask: **255.255.255.0**
5. Router: leave blank (if it refuses to save, enter 192.168.1.1)
6. Tap **Save**.
7. Open Safari and go to **http://192.168.1.100**

Two heads ups:
- While the iPad is set to Manual it loses internet, so keep this chat open on your phone.
- Once the UI loads, go to Settings / Network, set it back to **DHCP** or **Automatic**, save, and reboot the miner. Then put the iPad's Configure IP back to **Automatic**.

After the miner reboots, watch the LCD for its new 10.0.0.x address.

Tell me what Safari shows.
It worked thanks

Nice work, you did the tricky part.

Two bits of housekeeping:

1. Put the iPad's **Configure IP** back to **Automatic** so it gets internet again.
2. Make sure the miner is saved on **DHCP** and note the new 10.0.0.x address from the LCD.

Tip for next time: if you want a fixed address, do it as a DHCP reservation in your router rather than a static IP on the miner. Same result, and it cannot strand the unit.

JD still has the note about the reset button on your board revision, so you may get a short email from the team tomorrow after 10am ET. You can ignore it if all is well.

Anything else on the DC06, hashrate, pool or temps, just ask.
How come Home Screen shows best difficulty much lower than the one on pool website

Totally normal, they are counting different things.

1. The miner's number is local and resets. AxeOS style firmware keeps a best difficulty in flash, but a reboot, a settings wipe or a firmware update can clear it. You just rebooted and reconfigured the network, so that counter likely started fresh. The home screen often shows the **session** best, which is only since the last power on.
2. The pool's number is all time for your account or worker, kept server side since the day you started. It never resets when the miner does.
3. The pool may be totting up every worker under the same username. If you have ever run another miner or another Axe on that account, the pool shows the best across all of them.
4. Watch the units. 11.2M on one screen and 11.2G on the other are not the same thing, and pools vary on whether they show K, M, G or T.
5. Small print: the miner counts the real difficulty of every share it finds, while some pools only record shares at or above the vardiff level they set you. Usually a small gap, not a big one.

So: device best is "my best since boot", pool best is "your best ever". The pool number should always be the bigger one.

If your pool shows both an all time best and a 24 hour best, compare the device number against the 24 hour one, those should track each other closely.
